title: Erdős Problem #102: Maximum Collinear Points Forced by Many Rich Lines
description: Given n points with cn² lines containing ≥ 4 points, estimate h_c(n) = max collinear. Known: ≤ C√n. Erdős's √n lower conjecture disproved by Hunter. Open.

meta.author: Erdős–Purdy
originalContributions: Defined PointConfig structure for planar point configurations
Defined richLineCount counting lines with ≥ 4 collinear points
Defined maxCollinear as the supremum of collinear subset sizes

overview.historicalContext:
Erdős and Purdy posed this problem in their foundational survey of combinatorial geometry in the 1970s. The question asks: if a planar point set of size n has 'many' rich lines (at least cn² lines each containing ≥ 4 points), how large must the maximum collinear subset be?

Erdős conjectured that h_c(n) ≫ √n, meaning that many rich lines force a large collinear subset of roughly square-root size. This was disproved by Zach Hunter, who constructed lattice-point configurations showing h_c(n) ≪ n^{1/log(1/c)} — much slower growth than √n for small c. Hunter's construction exploits the arithmetic structure of integer lattice points to create many 4-point lines without any single line accumulating too many points.

The upper bound h_c(n) ≤ C√n follows from the Szemerédi–Trotter incidence theorem (1983), which bounds point-line incidences by O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + n + m). This is the main tool constraining how rich lines distribute among points. The fundamental question — whether h_c(n) → ∞ at all for fixed c — remains open and is closely connected to Problem #101 about the count of 4-point lines.
overview.problemStatement: Given n points in ℝ² with at least cn² lines containing ≥ 4 points, estimate h_c(n), the maximum collinear count. Is h_c(n) → ∞?
overview.proofStrategy: We formalize PointConfig for planar point sets, collinear₃ via the cross-product criterion, richLineCount counting 4-point lines, and maxCollinear as the supremum of collinear subset sizes. The divergence question, upper bound, Hunter's counterexample, and connections to Problem #101 and Szemerédi–Trotter are all axiomatized.
keyInsights: **Upper Bound √n**: h_c(n) ≤ C√n follows from Szemerédi–Trotter incidence bound — the key constraint on how rich lines can be distributed
**Hunter's Counterexample**: Disproved Erdős's √n lower conjecture using lattice-point configurations with h_c(n) ≪ n^{1/log(1/c)}, showing the truth is far below √n for small c
**Problem #101 Connection**: If h_c(n) → ∞, then the count of 4-point lines is o(n²) for no-5-collinear configurations — linking Problems #101 and #102
**Szemerédi–Trotter Foundation**: The incidence bound I(P,L) ≤ C(n^{2/3}m^{2/3}+n+m) is the primary tool constraining rich-line configurations
**Open Divergence**: Whether h_c(n) → ∞ at all remains the central open question — neither divergence nor bounded examples have been established

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #102 asks to estimate h_c(n), the maximum collinear count when cn² rich lines exist. The √n upper bound holds, but the conjectured √n lower bound was disproved by Hunter. Whether h_c(n) → ∞ remains open.
conclusion.implications: A resolution would complement Problem #101 and advance the Szemerédi–Trotter theory, illuminating the structure of point-line incidences in combinatorial geometry.
openQuestions: What is the true growth rate of h_c(n) between Hunter's bound and √n?
Can Hunter's lattice construction be improved or extended?
What is the precise relationship between c and the growth rate of h_c(n)?
Can algebraic geometry techniques (e.g., the polynomial method) make progress?
